tldr: Without any human demonstrations or intervention, this work uses sampling-based MPC as temporary scaffolding to master continuous in-hand object rotation on a 16-DoF hand after just 7 minutes of real-world online reinforcement learning.
hero_caption: Overall view of the proposed framework. The actor and critic are pretrained on a small set of trajectories collected by MPC. During online RL, MPC intervention is gradually decreased, ultimately acquiring a policy on hardware that is more than five times faster than MPC alone.
overview:
Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered robot hands is appealing, but training reinforcement learning (RL) directly on physical hardware from scratch suffers from frequent early failures (object drops), creating a severe burden of manual resets. While Sim-to-Real transfer and human teleoperation demonstrations have been used to circumvent this, discrepancies in contact dynamics and the high hardware cost of human teleoperation setups remain major bottlenecks.

To address this, the authors asked: "What if we use model predictive control (MPC) as temporary learning scaffolding so the robot can learn efficiently on hardware without human help?" Although MPC does not provide an optimal solution, it acts as a reliable guide that moves toward the task goal without dropping the object. In the proposed framework, only 20 trajectories (about 12 minutes) collected by MPC on hardware are used to pretrain the actor and critic. During online learning on the real robot, MPC guidance is intermittently interleaved while control gradually transitions to the learned policy.

In experiments on a 16-DoF Allegro Hand, the policy achieved a 100% success rate after just 7 minutes of online RL. With further learning, it reached more than five times the rotation speed of the original MPC controller (over 55 degrees per second) and demonstrated incredible durability and stability by completing 1,000 consecutive rotations (about 110 minutes) without a single drop. The framework also proved directly applicable to rapid adaptation to novel geometries and to precise goal-conditioned reorientation.
contributions: Proposed a new framework that uses sampling-based MPC as scaffolding to conduct safe and fast real-world RL without human demonstrations or corrective actions.
Clarified through ablations that the three roles of MPC—pretraining, retaining replay experience, and online guidance—act complementarily to drastically reduce object drops.

Demonstrated high reliability on hardware after just a few minutes of online learning, exceeding the teacher MPC's speed by more than five times and completing over 1,000 rotations (110+ minutes) with zero drops.
Showed versatility through rapid adaptation to unseen geometries (different-sized hexagonal prisms and cylinders) and high-precision goal-conditioned reorientation.

sections.heading: Why is real-world RL so hard on dexterous hands?
sections.summary: Because multi-fingered hand control is high-dimensional with complex contact dynamics, early exploration in real-world RL causes frequent object drops, putting a heavy reset burden on humans. Instead of relying on human demonstrations or teleoperation, this paper proposes an approach that introduces sampling-based MPC as temporary scaffolding to run safe, ultra-fast real-world learning.
sections.details:
In-hand object manipulation with multi-fingered hands is a representative contact-rich task where finger-object contacts constantly shift. When trying to solve this via real-world reinforcement learning (RL), early policies cannot properly grasp the object, dropping it to the floor within seconds. In the real world, failures directly translate to the cost of physical resets where humans must repeatedly pick up the object and return it to the starting position, severely degrading learning efficiency.

Conventionally, to circumvent this issue, common approaches relied on human teleoperation demonstrations (such as HIL-SERL) or transferring policies trained extensively in physics simulators to hardware (Sim-to-Real). However, teleoperating a dexterous hand requires bulky, specialized interfaces that impose heavy human burden, and simulators struggle to perfectly capture contact friction and subtle geometric discrepancies.

This motivated the authors to combine RL with model predictive control (MPC). Even if MPC cannot produce fully optimal behavior, it generates reasonably good actions that progress the task while avoiding drops. The authors' question was simple: "Instead of using sampling-based MPC as the final controller, what if we treat it as disposable scaffolding for early exploration to accelerate real-world RL without human assistance?"

This method leverages MPC trajectories across three stages: (1) pretraining, (2) retaining replay buffer data, and (3) guiding online exploration. As a result, the policy achieved a 100% success rate after just 7 minutes of online learning, keeping object drops down to an average of about three during training.

sections.heading: A three-stage framework using MPC as scaffolding to accelerate RL
sections.summary: The proposed method consists of three steps: (1) offline data collection via real-world MPC, (2) pretraining of the actor and critic, and (3) online SAC with progressively decreasing MPC guidance. By sharing the same joint position command interface, it achieves a seamless transition from the planner to the learned policy.
sections.details:
Here is an overview of the proposed framework and how each stage works.

### II-A Overall Architecture and MPC Controller
The system integrates sampling-based MPC as scaffolding for off-policy reinforcement learning (Soft Actor-Critic: SAC). On the MPC side, a digital twin built in MuJoCo is synchronized with real-world sensor information, and the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) optimizes joint motion primitives alongside residual sampling. Both MPC and SAC share the exact same 16-joint position command interface (10 Hz). Therefore, regardless of which controller generated the data, transitions can be stored in the same replay buffer and used for learning.

### II-B Offline MPC Data Collection and Pretraining
Running MPC on hardware, the system collects 20 trajectories that complete the desired rotation (about 12 minutes). Using this data, the actor and critic are initialized prior to online training.
- **Actor Pretraining**: Rather than simple behavioral cloning (BC), the stochastic policy's standard deviation (std) head has its final layer weights set to zero and bias fixed to a constant, preserving normalized randomness necessary for exploration. Additionally, softmax-weighted sampling based on episode returns and epsilon clipping on target actions ensure focused training on high-quality behaviors.
- **Critic Pretraining**: The critic is trained using a Soft-SARSA objective with an ensemble of 10 target critics. Incorporating the entropy term of the frozen BC actor here guarantees mathematical and structural consistency with subsequent online SAC.

### II-C & II-D Mixed Replay and MPC Scheduling
During online training, 30% of each minibatch is sampled from the fixed offline MPC buffer, and the remaining 70% from the newly collected online buffer. Because MPC serves as a good guide but is not optimal, keeping its ratio lower encourages the policy to improve beyond MPC.

Furthermore, during online exploration, the probability of MPC guidance is gradually decreased. Starting from an initial execution probability $p_0=0.5$, the policy's execution probability is linearly scaled up to 1.0 over 6,000 steps (about 10 minutes in real time). To prevent finger chattering caused by rapid switching, controller selection is performed in chunks of 40 steps (4 seconds), which is an important practical design choice.

sections.heading: Mastered in 7 minutes, with extreme stability over 1,000 rotations without a drop
sections.summary: Real-world evaluation was conducted using a 16-DoF Allegro Hand. The proposed method mastered the rotation task in just 7 minutes of online learning, reaching over five times the rotation speed of MPC. It also demonstrated remarkable reliability with zero drops over 1,000 consecutive rotations (110+ minutes), and showed high adaptability to new geometries and goal reorientation tasks.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B Experimental Setup and Ablation Results
The hardware setup consists of a 16-DoF Allegro Hand mounted on a Franka FR3 arm, with OptiTrack tracking object pose. The primary task is continuous in-hand rotation of a 45 mm hexagonal prism.

Ablation experiments (Fig. F3) investigated the three components: retained MPC replay (R), pretraining (P), and online guidance (G).
- **Full method (R+P+G)**: Achieved 100% success across 5 consecutive evaluation trials after just 7.4 minutes of online learning. Training drops averaged only 3 across 3 trials.
- **No Pretraining (R+G)**: Required about 16 minutes to reach success, and drops increased to an average of 17. This highlights that pretraining significantly speeds up initial progress and dramatically cuts down resets.
- **No Guidance (R+P)**: Required 25.8 minutes to succeed, with increased variance across trials.
- **RL Only**: Failed to succeed even once after 45 minutes, dropping the object 181 times. This demonstrates that real-world learning is practically impossible without MPC scaffolding.

### III-B 2 Long-Horizon Evaluation and Exceeding MPC Speed
The trained policy was compared against direct MPC execution and a Sim-to-Real PPO policy trained with domain randomization over 15 million steps (Fig. F4a).
- Direct MPC: Had zero drops, but rotation speed was slow at $9.9^{\circ}/\mathrm{s}$.
- Sim-to-Real PPO: While achieving 100% success in simulation, it failed 8 out of 28 times on hardware (71% success rate) and achieved only $31.5^{\circ}/\mathrm{s}$.
- Proposed method: Achieved 100% success across 20 trials, reaching a speed of $55.3^{\circ}/\mathrm{s}$—more than five times faster than its MPC instructor.
Even more impressive was its long-term reliability. When tested on 1,000 continuous rotations (about 110 minutes of continuous operation), the policy ran to completion without dropping the object a single time (Fig. F4b).

### III-C & III-D Geometry Adaptation and Goal-Conditioned Reorientation
When transferred to other object geometries (a 35 mm hexagonal prism and a 55 mm cylinder), the system adapted rapidly through additional online learning with MPC guidance, without recollecting offline data or retraining from scratch (Fig. F6). Rotation speed increased by 45% to 84% compared to pre-adaptation levels.
Beyond continuous rotation, the framework was evaluated on goal-conditioned reorientation to specified target angles ($\pm 20^{\circ}$) (Fig. F7). After 45 minutes of real-world training, the final error shrank to just a few degrees, achieving precise control with 100 successes out of 103 trials (97.1% success rate, zero drops).

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: By treating sampling-based MPC as learning scaffolding, this work realizes an extremely efficient and robust real-world RL framework requiring no human intervention or demonstrations. It offers a practical paradigm that merges the reliability of model-based control with the optimization power of reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated a real-world reinforcement learning framework for challenging dexterous contact manipulation that leverages sampling-based MPC not as a permanent controller, but as temporary learning scaffolding.

Through the three complementary roles of retaining MPC replay, pretraining, and online guidance, the system minimizes human reset effort (to just a few drops) while acquiring proficient behaviors after only a dozen minutes of physical contact. Furthermore, the resulting policy is not constrained by the performance limits of its MPC teacher, manipulating objects safely and stably at more than five times the speed.

For complex robotic systems where setting up human teleoperation is difficult, using a coarse model-based controller as scaffolding and refining it directly on hardware provides a powerful design paradigm for future robot learning.

takeaways: While MPC used as an end controller is often slow due to computational overhead and modeling errors, using it purely as early exploration scaffolding allows training an ultra-fast, stable policy directly on hardware.
Pretraining (P), retaining replay data (R), and online guidance (G) serve distinct roles; combining pretraining with online guidance is especially key to drastically cutting resets (drops).
Even on a 16-DoF dexterous hand where human teleoperation demonstrations are difficult, real-world RL can be completed autonomously as long as a basic physics-based MPC controller is available.
limitations: Synchronizing the digital twin to run MPC relies on an external high-precision motion capture system (OptiTrack); achieving full autonomy with vision-only observations remains future work.
Coarse model information such as approximate geometry and mass properties is required beforehand, meaning the method cannot be applied immediately from scratch to completely unknown objects.
Designing task-specific motion primitives and cost functions to support MPC's sampling-based search is still required to a certain extent for each task.
